title: The memory-safety redesign (preview)
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA. This lesson goes further: it needs `LangVersion` set to `preview` even on the .NET 11 SDK, so treat it as a look at where the language is heading.

C# 15 begins a multi-release effort to tie `unsafe` to operations that actually access unmanaged memory, rather than to the mere presence of pointer types. With the preview language version, declaring a pointer, taking an address with `&`, `fixed`, converting `stackalloc` to a pointer and `sizeof` on unmanaged types no longer require an unsafe context.

Dereferencing still does: `*p`, `p->member`, `p[i]` and function-pointer calls need `unsafe`. The new `unsafe(expression)` form creates an unsafe context for one expression, useful in field initializers, constructor initializers and catch filters where an unsafe block cannot appear.

Opting into the updated rules (the `updated-memory-safety-rules` feature) also makes `unsafe` on a member mean 'requires unsafe': the obligation passes to callers, who must call it from an unsafe context. A `safe` contextual keyword marks `extern` members and certain fields as safe. The compiler records the choice with `MemorySafetyRulesAttribute`.

The goal is that reviewers can find every memory-accessing operation by searching for `unsafe`. Until the feature ships in a released language version, keep production code on stage 13's rules and check the C# 15/16 notes for the final design.
challenge: Without an unsafe block around the declaration, take the address of a local double and print the value doubled using a single unsafe(...) expression for the dereference.
question: Under the C# 15 preview rules, which operation still requires an unsafe context?
wrong: Declaring a variable of type int*
reasoning: The redesign keeps unsafe for operations that access memory; creating pointers and pinning are relaxed.
